opus-5.5.text:
It was a real shift in how I had to think. At MIT, especially in math, you're trained to look for the one correct proof. There's a ground truth, and once you've shown it, you're done. Law is almost the opposite. You're taught to argue both sides, and the "answer" often depends on interpretation, precedent, and how persuasive you are. At first that felt a bit uncomfortable to me, almost slippery.

Over time, though, I started to see a lot of structure in it. Legal reasoning has its own logic: you have rules, you have cases that act a bit like lemmas, and you're building an argument step by step from them. The difference is that the axioms aren't fixed. They're shaped by people, by history, by values. That made me appreciate how much of human reasoning happens in spaces that aren't fully formalized.

Honestly, that experience fed back into how I think about math and AI. It made me ask: what does it actually mean for reasoning to be rigorous? In math we have formal verification, where you can check every step. In law you can't really do that. So it gave me a deeper respect for formal systems, and also a clearer sense of why being able to verify reasoning matters so much, especially as we build AI systems that are supposed to reason for us.

And on a personal level, it taught me to communicate differently. Mathematicians can be quite terse. In law, you have to bring people along, anticipate objections, and tell a coherent story. That's turned out to be surprisingly useful, whether I'm writing papers, talking to investors, or building a team.

fable-5.1.text:
It was honestly a bit of a shock to the system at first. At MIT, everything I did in math and in the lab had this structure where you start from axioms or from data, you build up a chain of reasoning, and at the end there is something you can check. Either the proof holds or it doesn't. Either the experiment replicates or it doesn't. Law doesn't work like that. The first weeks I kept looking for the "answer" in the cases and getting frustrated that there wasn't one, that two judges could look at the same facts and reach opposite conclusions, and both opinions would be treated as legitimate.

But once I stopped fighting it, I actually found it really intellectually satisfying, because what law trains you to do is reason under ambiguity. You learn to hold multiple framings at once, to argue the other side's best case before you argue your own, and to pay attention to language in a way that scientists often don't. A single word in a statute can change everything. I think that made me a more careful thinker, not a less rigorous one.

The other thing that struck me is how much law is really about institutions and incentives rather than about rules on paper. Coming from engineering, you think about systems, and I started to see the legal system as a system too, with feedback loops, failure modes, and places where it's badly designed. That perspective turned out to be very useful later when I started thinking about AI, because the hard questions there aren't really technical. They're questions about who decides, who's accountable, and what happens when a system behaves in ways nobody anticipated. Having spent time in both worlds, I feel like I can translate between people who speak only one of those languages, and that translation is something I think we desperately need more of right now.

r001.rationale: The response describes law school as a shock and discusses ambiguity, but does not say that homework consisting solely of assigned reading was new to Carina when she entered law school.

astra-6.text:
Coming from science and engineering, I found studying law to be a shift in how you approach a question. In a technical problem, you try to make the assumptions precise and work toward a solution. In law, the assumptions themselves can be what’s contested: What does this language mean? Which facts matter? What should the rule accomplish?

I think the analytical habits carry over, but you have to become more comfortable with ambiguity. You can have two carefully reasoned arguments that lead to different conclusions. That pushes you to think about not just whether an argument is internally consistent, but also the values and consequences behind it.

sol-6.1.text:
Coming from science and engineering at MIT, I found the shift to law interesting because it required a different kind of precision. In a technical problem, you often start with explicit assumptions and work toward a solution. In law, you also have to ask how the assumptions are framed, what a particular word means, and which facts matter.

There’s still a lot of analytical reasoning, so that part felt familiar. What challenged me was learning to work with ambiguity—to understand how two people could reason carefully and reach different conclusions. It pushed me to think more about the institutions and human judgments behind the rules.
